title: Mirror a binary tree
prompt:
A display team wants a binary tree flipped left-to-right, as if seen in a mirror: return the tree where every node's left and right children have been swapped.

- Nodes have val, left and right (child node or null). In Python they are dicts: node["left"].
- Return the root of the mirrored tree using the same node shape (null / None for an empty tree). You may modify the input in place or build a new tree.
- 0 to 10,000 nodes; depth at most 500; values are integers between -10^4 and 10^4 and may repeat.
hints: If you already had the mirrored left and right subtrees, how would you attach them to the root?
Mirroring is a local operation: swap the two children of every node, in any visiting order.
Push the root on a stack; pop a node, swap its left and right, then push its non-null children until the stack is empty.

solution.py:
def mirror_tree(root):
    stack = [root] if root else []
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        node["left"], node["right"] = node["right"], node["left"]
        stack.extend(child for child in (node["left"], node["right"]) if child)
    return root
solution.explanation: A tree is mirrored exactly when every node has its two children swapped, so the order in which nodes are visited does not matter. An explicit stack visits each node once and avoids recursion-depth limits on tall trees.

complexity.notes: The DFS stack holds O(h) pending nodes for a depth-first order; a BFS queue would hold O(w), the widest level. The swap is in place, so no new nodes are allocated.

followUps: How would you check whether a tree is symmetric (equal to its own mirror) without building the mirror?
